openQuestions.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
County tax and exoneration lists for this period exist and are reachable via curated external links.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes moved from the Diocese of Philadelphia to the Diocese of Scranton in 1868. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Pennsylvania County Marriages: Martin Kearney m. Bridget (Doyle) Halloran, 1879, Schuylkill County. Confirms Bridget's second marriage and that her first married surname was Doyle, maiden name Halloran. Found incidentally while researching an unrelated question; not part of any plan.

query.description: 1900 census page image, Schuylkill County, PA - Kearney household, fertility columns

items.notes: Original 1900 census image for the Kearney household: 'Mother of how many children' = 9; 'Number of these children living' = 2. Indicates Bridget bore ~9 children, most likely during the earlier Doyle marriage, with only 2 surviving to 1900. Only one of the two, Ellen Doyle, has been identified by name so far. Roughly 7-8 children remain unidentified/undocumented.

Pennsylvania County Marriages: entry for Ellen Doyle's own marriage, with her parents recorded as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Independently identifies the first husband's given name as JOHN Doyle. Found incidentally; not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Highest-priority item: the 1860 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1473181, indexed, 27.5M records) is the most likely single record to enumerate multiple Doyle children at once. John Doyle was still living in 1860 (he predeceased Bridget's 1879 remarriage), so he would appear as household head with Bridget and any children born through the 1850s. The 1860 census does not record relationship to head, so all persons in the household must be examined. Search surname variants Doyel and Doyal alongside Doyle; Halloran/Hallaren for Bridget. This is the anchor census from which the family's composition can be established.

Complements pli_001: Ancestry's 1850 US Federal Census for Schuylkill County (collection 1276, returned by external_links_search) may show the Doyle household a decade earlier, before some children were born. If the family arrived in the anthracite coal region by 1850, this census provides the earliest snapshot — any older children visible in 1860 should appear here too, with slightly younger ages, helping to anchor birth-year estimates. FamilySearch did not return a 1850 census collection in the surveyed scope, so Ancestry is the primary repository for this year.

The 1870 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1438024, indexed, 38.5M records) would capture children born in the 1860s not yet visible in 1860, and provide a decade-later view of children found in pli_001. By 1870 Bridget had likely borne 7–9 of her 9 children; John Doyle would still be head of household (he died before 1879). This census added columns for parents' birthplaces (Ireland expected), enabling additional confirmation of the family's identity. Search Doyle surname variants and Bridget Halloran/Hallaren as spouse.

The 1880 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1417683, indexed, 50.1M records) is the post-Doyle census: Bridget remarried Martin Kearney in 1879, so she appears as Bridget Kearney. Search the Kearney household — surviving Doyle children still at home would be listed as stepchildren or children with relationship recorded (1880 is the first census to record every person's relationship to the head). Also search independently for Ellen Doyle (now married to an unknown husband) as her own household head or wife. The log_002 image read identified the Kearney household, but an indexed name search is still warranted for any Doyle children who had left home by then.

The indexed Schuylkill County Church Records (FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, personCount 982,415, dated 1708–1985) are the primary pre-1906 birth and death source for an Irish Catholic family in Pennsylvania — civil registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001). entry.rationale: Norway Census 1801 (FS col 3733603) is indexed and free. Hoval born ~1780 would be approximately 21 years old in 1801. A census entry gives 1801 residence and may list household members, employer, or co-residents that corroborate identity across time. Digitalarkivet also hosts the 1801 census at digitalarkivet.no/en/census/search/1801 as an alternate access point if the FS result is ambiguous.

Norwegian conscription rolls (lægdsruller) began in 1789; a male born ~1780 would be enrolled at approximately age 9 (from ~1789). Per the record-type guide, lægdsruller are required for a Norwegian male parentage question — each boy is entered directly under his father's name, making the roll direct parentage evidence. Session notations also track the father's death and the boy's residence and occupation. Per loc_002, access is via Riksarkivet (riksarkivet.no) and Digitalarkivet (search sources → lægdsruller / 'Regnskap og skattemateriale'). Date range bounded by Hoval's plausible enrollment age under his father's name, not his own later career.

Per the record-type guide, a dedicated item for the parents' marriage is required on every parentage plan. Hoval's parents married before his ~1780 birth; searching Kongsberg marriages 1760–1790 (FS col 1468080, Norway Marriages 1660–1926) may yield: (a) the register entry confirming the parental couple as a unit; (b) the mother's maiden name, which censuses and death records typically omit; and (c) the marriage date, which by its proximity to Hoval's ~1780 birth corroborates the father's identity. Date range bounded by the parents' plausible lifespan (father likely born by ~1755, marriage before ~1780 birth), not by Hoval's own research window. Note the limit: the marriage record proves the parents married — it is not by itself evidence that Hoval is their child; his own baptism entry naming him as their son remains the needed direct link.

The Trysilboka (Lillevold et al., FS Family History Library, call no. 948.23/T2 D2l, multiple vols.) is a published farm genealogy for Trysil with personal name indexes in vols. 1–3 and 7–8 (per loc_001). The alias 'Ziener' is distinctive and uncommon in Trysil — it would stand out in a farm-book index. The compiled work may identify the Ziener/Hansen household and provide secondary-source data on Hoval's birthplace, parents, and family connections that can be verified against originals. Treat the Trysilboka as a source of leads, not concluded evidence. Also check slekt1.com/index.php/bygdeboker for any online access to this or related Trysil bygdebøker.
